name: Molecular Systems
tagline: Systems chemistry, molecular machines, and emergent chemical behavior.
seo_title: Molecular Systems — paper summaries, news & innovations | Chemisters
seo_description: Follow Chemisters Molecular Systems on LinkedIn and Facebook: paper summaries, news and innovations in systems chemistry, self-replication, molecular machines and emergent behaviour.

definition.lead: Molecular Systems studies collections of molecules that interact to produce behaviour no single molecule shows: self-replication, molecular machines, networks and emergent function.
definition.body: Life is the ultimate molecular system. Chemists now build simpler ones in the lab, from self-replicating molecules to motors and pumps, to understand how complex behaviour emerges and to create adaptive materials.

facts.label: the Miller–Urey experiment makes amino acids from simple gases
Günter von Kiedrowski reports a self-replicating molecule

branches.name: Systems chemistry
branches.summary: Networks of interacting molecules studied as a whole.
branches.example: Reaction networks that show life-like behaviour.

branches.name: Self-replication
branches.summary: Molecules that make copies of themselves.

branches.name: Dynamic combinatorial chemistry
branches.summary: Libraries of molecules that reshuffle and adapt.
branches.example: A library that amplifies the best binder for a template.

branches.name: Fuel-driven assembly
branches.summary: Structures that exist only while energy is supplied.
branches.example: Assemblies that fall apart when the fuel runs out.

branches.name: Molecular computing
branches.example: DNA used to solve a routing problem.

timeline.title: Building blocks from gases
timeline.text: The Miller–Urey experiment produces amino acids.
timeline.why: Chemistry could plausibly lead toward life.

timeline.title: Catalytic RNA
timeline.text: Thomas Cech discovers that RNA can catalyse reactions.
timeline.why: Supports the idea of an early RNA world.

timeline.title: A self-replicating molecule
timeline.text: Günter von Kiedrowski reports a short nucleic acid that templates its own formation.

timeline.title: Synthetic self-replicators
timeline.text: Julius Rebek's group reports a self-replicating synthetic molecule.

timeline.title: Computing with DNA
timeline.text: Leonard Adleman uses DNA molecules to solve a small routing problem.

timeline.title: A molecular motor
timeline.text: Ben Feringa's group builds a light-driven rotary motor.
timeline.why: Directional motion at the molecular scale.

timeline.title: Replicators that emerge
timeline.text: Sijbren Otto's group sees self-replicators emerge spontaneously from a dynamic library.
timeline.why: Selection and replication from simple chemistry.

timeline.title: Molecular machines
timeline.text: Nobel Prize to Sauvage, Stoddart and Feringa.

Splits into two randomly
Needs a cell to copy it

quiz.q: The RNA world hypothesis proposes that early life…
options: Used RNA both to store information and to catalyse reactions
Used only proteins, with no nucleic acids at all
Arrived on Earth fully formed from space
Used DNA only, with proteins appearing later
quiz.explain: Ribozymes show RNA can be a catalyst.

options: A mixture of molecules exchanging parts reversibly, whose composition shifts in response to a template
A shelf of chemistry books in a university library

A database of reactions extracted from the literature
A continuous supply of energy (fuel)
No energy at all
Freezing temperatures
A magnetic field
quiz.explain: Like living cells, they stop when the fuel runs out.

quiz.q: What did Leonard Adleman do in 1994?
options: Used DNA to solve a computing problem
Built the first chemistry robot
Sequenced the first human genome
Made the first synthetic protein
quiz.explain: A small directed Hamiltonian path problem.

options: An energy input and a mechanism that makes motion directional
Only random collisions with solvent molecules
A tiny battery attached to each molecule
No energy at all, since molecules always move
quiz.explain: Random motion alone cannot do useful work.

A catalyst destroys itself
No catalyst is needed

quiz.explain: Positive feedback: the more you have, the faster you make more.

quiz.q: What did the Miller–Urey experiment produce?
options: Amino acids from simple gases
Living cells
Complete DNA strands
Folded proteins
quiz.explain: Sparks in a mixture of gases and water.

options: To understand how life-like behaviour can emerge from chemistry
To replace biology with simpler systems
Because they are easy and quick to publish

quiz.q: Why do ribozymes support the RNA world idea?
options: They show RNA can act as a catalyst
They are proteins that copy RNA
They contain DNA instead of RNA
They are minerals found in clay
quiz.explain: RNA could have done both jobs before proteins evolved.

quiz.q: Feringa's molecular motor is powered by…
options: Light
Sound
Gravity
Static electricity
quiz.explain: Light-driven isomerization followed by thermal steps.
